utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. If you could kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are present. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes and Mr. Ostojic. Prosecution is represented by Mr. McCloskey. The witness is already in his place. So I take it there are no preliminaries. Yes, Mr. Krgovic, I spoke too soon. One moment. Let me just have a word with the witness and then of course you will proceed with your cross-examination. Colonel, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have some further cross-examinations today. Mr. Krgovic for General Gvero will continue his and then I suppose he will be followed by Mr. Bourgon, who would be I suppose the last one to cross-examine you, after which there is going to be a re-examination, as we were told yesterday. We'll make to effort to finish with your testimony today, if that is possible. May I just remind you of two things, the first being that you are still testifying pursuant to your solemn declaration to testify the truth, and also wish to remind you of my explanation regarding your rights in relation to what would seem to you to be incriminatory questions. Having said that, I now give the floor to Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Krgovic. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Before I move on to my next topic, I would like to clarify something that was recorded on page 84 in line 17 through 20. When I was asking you about the big chess field, you actually answered that General Gvero tried to copy the chess field from the hotel in Kupare in the hotel in Han Pijesak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Correction in the transcript, please, from the hotel in Kupare to the hotel in Han Pijesak. Thank you, Colonel. I'll move on to another topic. The Prosecutor, during the interview, showed you a document and you discussed this document with the Prosecutor during that interview. Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P45? Look at the document and particularly the number in the left-hand side corner. The number belongs to your body, the body that you worked in?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was Miletic who worked in that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The operations body?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the operations body. But I was in a different unit. I was a part -- a member of the armoured unit, which is entirely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can the document please be zoomed in so that the witness -- or rather zoomed out to show the witness the entire document? Thank you. Colonel, in answering the Prosecutor's questions, you said that this document had been drafted by an operative. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in on the introduction, on the two last paragraphs of the introduction, scroll a little bit further down? Now, a little bit up. A bit more. Can you now see this part?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a combat order and I'm interested in this introduction. Do you agree that these goals and tasks contained in this order were provided by the commander?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. Based on this first sentence, I can see immediately that instructions were provided, i.e., that an order or rather an instruction was given so as to enable the person to draft the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who was in a position to provide instructions for the drafting of this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was exclusively the commander who could provide instructions to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment on the 13th of July the commander was in the area of responsibility, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that for sure. I don't know where he was. I wasn't with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He was in the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was in the territory of Republika Srpska. Wherever he was, there was his forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you have heard -- we have heard from you, actually what we heard yesterday, as far as I understood, this is a very complex combat order and in order to draft this order, it took skills and knowledge General Gvero did not possess those skills and knowledge required to draft such a combat decision, combat order. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is going so fast that the interpreters are having a hard time keeping up, plus it's very compound. It can be done so it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can help you very little on your last -- I think that depends on Mr. Krgovic himself. Please try to simplify your questions by splitting them up in simple rather than compound ones. That's number 1. The second thing, I can of course help. And I invite you, Colonel, and you, Mr. Krgovic, please, to slow down. I could sense the difficulty that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- interpreters are encountering and I tried them both, the French and the English channels, and it seems to be the same. So please try to make everybody's life a bit simpler. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I try, Your Honour. I apologise. [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown the following page of the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in the signature block, the name that is typed is assistant commander, General Colonel Milan Gvero?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There is no stamp, there is no signature. In my view this should be a telegram that was received by another unit. This is not an original telegram.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Can you bear with me just a second? This is a document that was received. You can see it in the stamp. The word that is encircled means received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When such documents were sent, and when somebody signs on behalf of the person who is not there, this cannot be seen in such telegrams?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can't see that because these are usually signatures that are illegible and the only thing that is being encrypted or coded is the things that are typed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which makes me conclude that although his name is typed here, this doesn't mean that General Gvero signed this document.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But it is possible that somebody else signed on behalf of General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, I can't tell you anything for a fact. Anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because that's a very general way of explaining things, "Everything is possible." Wouldn't it be correct to say that in your country, and in your language, if someone is signing for someone else, he would put the word "za" before the name of the person for whom he is signing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you put "za" and then you sign, and the signature is usually illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So if there is no "za," the indication is that it is not signed by someone on behalf of someone else, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the person who signed the document is the person whose name is typed out on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if you can find the letters "SV" in the document, what would that mean?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would mean in his own hand, that the person has written the document in his own hand, i.e. signed the document in his own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, the "SV" is missing from the document.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a correction for the transcript. The letters that I mentioned were "SR" when I put my question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, one more question. At the time when you were in the operations room, did you see General Gvero ever drafting such orders throughout the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never drafted anything remotely similar to this. If anybody claimed anything differently, it would be a lie, it wouldn't be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that General Gvero was not capable of drafting any such thing, did you mean that he did not have the skill, the knowledge and the experience for something like that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important thing is that he did not have any experience in dealing with such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And certainly the information about the developments?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can't say anything about the information. The information arrived by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, just one more thing, let me ask you. In July 1995, who was replacing General Gvero, i.e. who was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Savo Sokanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He was in the building next door?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the left side, the last office in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in addition to what you told us yesterday, in response to my questions and the Prosecutor's questions about the role of General Gvero, you don't have any other information as to what he had done in his body, you were not aware of any documents, you don't know any details of what he was doing as a member of his body?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the document that I've just shown you, you never saw it before the Prosecutor showed it to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you are not aware of any document that General Gvero might have received or sent or any such correspondence that was drafted in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And General Gvero did not have to explain himself to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Any other documents, if anybody asked you about it, you would have to guess, you don't have any immediate experience of any document that Gvero drafted?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would Gvero show a head of a branch what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Judges, good afternoon, colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. I just have two quick questions for you and these are based on your experience and of course I take these questions on the basis also of the visit you made in the area of Zvornik Brigade. So you recall what visit I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you're talking about my travel to the front line on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Colonel. I would just like you to confirm that when officers are dispatched by the Main Staff to assess the situation within a subordinate unit, would you agree with me that the commander of the subordinate unit or in this case, for example, the deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade, who will receive the visiting officers of the Main Staff would be expected to cooperate and to provide any information that was requested. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that if the visiting officers from the Main Staff have been asked to look into the operational situation of the subordinate unit, that it would be normal for them to look at the duty officer's notebook or duty officer's diary in order to familiarise themselves with what happened within the subordinate unit? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The logbook would not be the place for that. The logbook would record the information that was received the previous evening from the subordinated units. As for the ongoing situation, you have to wait until the following evening to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe, Colonel, my question was not clear enough. If you have been asked to look into what happened before within the subordinate unit, one of the places you could find this information is indeed into the duty officer's notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the reports of the subordinated commands that we discussed at length yesterday, we can get that information, and as for the subordinated units, the level of the brigade, the Main Staff, I would leave that to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your answer. What I'm trying to get at is you are an experienced military officer who was working at the -- within the Main Staff. All I'm asking you is on the basis of your experience, whether, if you want to have information as to what happened within a subordinate unit, one of the places you can find this information is in the duty officer's notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question, Colonel, is simply the following: If we are looking at the situation of the officer within the subordinate unit, he would expect you to look at the duty officer's notebook in order to find what happened in the unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In practice, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe again my question was not clear. We are looking at the situation whereby senior officers from the Main Staff are visiting a subordinate unit. I'm simply suggesting to you that either the commander or the deputy commander of the subordinate unit, they would expect that if I have visitors from the Main Staff, they might very well look into the duty officer's notebook. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, when an officer arrives from the Main Staff to a subordinate unit, the commander or the officer that he finds on the spot briefs him on the situation in the unit. No books or logbooks are inspected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I just want to double -- make sure, make double sure with you, Mr. Sarapa, that you don't want to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We don't wish to examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's back to you, Mr. McCloskey, for your re-examination. I just want to confirm, since I received three different versions in the course of the day, in the course of the morning, that you have got the latest list of intended Prosecution exhibits. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure we all have, because those of us on the Defence side of the Court have had some discussions about this document. Let me say for our part, and I think this is the stance that we are all taking, we're going to allow for Mr. McCloskey to begin, that doesn't mean to say we won't object as he goes along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But we are grateful to him for putting us on notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could resolve this legal issue be -- and not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What legal issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The issue that the counsel is referring to. I think it might have to do with 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, you have to speak out and tell us precisely what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can intervene at this time we have been given a list of 23 documents. It appears to us to the best of our knowledge after making a series of verifications that at least 11 of these documents are new documents that were never included in the Prosecution's list of Rule 65 ter list. And when we look at the nature of these documents that would be the basis of any argument we would make, we look at the nature of these documents we cannot find a reason why they would not have been added beforehand and we believe that this is something, these documents should not be used, despite the Court's ruling on this issue and of course we can expand more on our arguments. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's clear. On the other hand, will you be using all these documents or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I never know really in redirect. I had time, I had a list, so I gave it to them. That's not something we normally do or have time but I'd like to respond but I think the witness really shouldn't be here to have to listen to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect, I'm quite anxious the Court doesn't deal with this on a general basis. The Gvero Defence wish to deal with it on an individual document-by-document basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how it will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed our grounds for objection are not just in relation to the fact that the document has not been on the 65 ter list but there is no point in making any submission until my learned friend has been given a chance to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. And our position, so we are going to -- any further discussion on this for the time being, is we'll wait until we hear an objection and then we will deal with each objection as it arises. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's been several arguments that have made. I have not responded to them. I would like to have a chance to respond to them but it's not appropriate that I do it in front of this witness, nor -- and I would prefer that we got the big picture, as Mr. Bourgon brought up, out of the way and that he's not being negated by his colleague. Because I understand that issues should be ripe before they are dealt with, but Mr. Bourgon brought up an issue. There is a suggestion here that this -- these documents perhaps were improperly brought to you and I would like to just, you know, deal with that and not have to ask the witness to leave in the middle of his redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but I don't think there is a possibility of discussing this globally or holistically before we start and we come to the particular documents because it's not just the principle relating to the non-inclusion of these documents on the 65 ter list that is involved here and on which we have already decided for the purpose of redirect. You know that we have handed down a decision and we are not prepared to reopen discussion on that, but as I understand both Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Josse, there are other aspects that they wish to raise and I see no point in raising them now, not even knowing if you will be using these documents or if an objection will be forthcoming in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President. I think they would like to revisit that issue but I guess we'll have to wait and see. I appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the first one does have a number so -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you for your patience. You had talked a little bit about recently about some of what you believed General Gvero's position involved, and I want to ask you to take a look at a document that helps define the -- I believe it helps define the position of morale, religious and Legal Officers. It's number 2512, and I've got a hard copy of it for you to take a look at. It's also in e-court but it's kind of long. It comes out of the Main Staff. So I think you may have heard about it. I don't want to spend a whole lot of time with it but it's dated the 10th of February 1995 and it talks about the authority and the filling of personnel vacancies for the organs, the morale, religious and legal affairs. And then it outlines right there on that first page, five different parts of that job, as I understand it, and I just wanted to ask you about your understanding of this, and then as it goes on, it gets a little more detail on each of those five responsibilities. So if we could, as a senior officer of the Main Staff of the VRS, that has been identified by yourself as an expert in artillery and armour, let's take a look at just the -- of the five things they talk about, the first one is moral tradition and cultural activities. I won't ask you about that. Number 2 is informing and psychological propaganda activities. Can you tell us briefly your understanding of what informing and psychological propaganda activities are? And if you want to take a look at the detailed part of that -- in fact, let me just mention those. I'll tell you which ones we'll talk about, then we will go to the detailed part. So The first one I'm going to ask you about is the propaganda activities. I'm not going to ask you about number 3, cooperation with the authority organs and other social subjects. Then it says, as well as international organisations and institutions. That one, I will ask you about. So these two. So, first, let's go to number 2, that's on page 4 of the English, and it's under section 2(B) and it says, "Psychological and propaganda activities directed towards our units and population as well as the units and the population of the opponent." And it goes down -- and I'm -- it's right above paragraph 3 where it actually talks a little bit more detail about this, and it says, "Gather information with the purpose of psychological and propaganda activities on enemy forces and population and secure their presentation through the centre for IPPT in order to weakening combat morale of the population and enemy army." Then the next one says, "Realise tight cooperation with intelligence, security and other organs of the command in order to change information and mutual coordination of measures, activities and behaviour." First of all, to your knowledge as a member of the Main Staff, is this propaganda definition that I think is part of the definition they are talking about of the brigade and corps, does this form part of the definition of the job that General Gvero was doing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is an objection. I wanted to allow my learned friend to finish the question. The witness certainly shouldn't hear the objection. I agree with my learned friend about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. McCloskey, are you aware of [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you aware if Mr. Trkulja understands English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think he may understand a little but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trkulja, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless if anyone of you insists that he leaves the courtroom, we'll do that. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In other words, he can stay here? Okay. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To begin with, that extraordinarily long question deals in part with this document. If, and I'll come to this in a moment, my learned friend is seriously re-examining in relation to the document then the witness is going to need to read the document properly and to have selected snippets of it; in the way that has been done is not satisfactory. But secondly, this is no more than a veiled attempt, through cross -- through re-examination, to introduce this particular document. My learned friend could ask the witness in the most general terms about propaganda perhaps and the role of General Gvero in relation to that particular aspect of his work, but why does he need to show him the document? The document, as I've already said, in effect is intended to lead the witness. The document is in effect there to try and introduce the document into this case through the witness, and in our submission, that isn't acceptable. So I accept that what I've said is mutually inconsistent but I'm putting it as an either/or submission. In other words, our first submission is that he shouldn't be allowed to ask these questions using this document at all. I repeat this is no more than an obvious attempt to introduce the document. But if the Court is against the Defence so far as that's concerned, then we say the witness should be entitled to read this document from beginning to end. He's very sensibly starting to do that now, unsurprisingly. I make no real complaint about that. It's rather interesting that he is doing that. It supports what I'm saying in many ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Josse. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, since this objection came with the first question, could we ask the witness to leave? I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trkulja, Mr. Trkulja, we need to discuss a few things which cannot be discussed or which are better not discussed in your presence. I suggest -- I'm asking Madam Usher to accompany you out of the courtroom. This will take only a short time and you will be back soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what my learned friend has just said and inviting the witness to leave, could I also make this general observation which I think will amount to an objection? I invite the Prosecution to inform the Court where this line of re-examination is going. The questions that Mr. Krgovic asked of the witness were no more than those which have previously in effect been asked of other Main Staff witnesses and in our submission, what the Prosecution should not be allowed to do, and they have sought to do this on a number of occasions in this case, is use re-examination as a back door for the examination-in-chief which, for whatever reason, they did not do either properly, fully or in a way that they wanted at the time. Re-examination is not intended to plug the gaps in their case. And, again, my learned friend gives the game away by producing this very long list of documents. We do appreciate that he's done that and indeed Mr. Krgovic had an advantage over Madam Fauveau. At least Mr. Krgovic had an opportunity to see the documents before he finished his cross-examination. I have to accept that on the Gvero Defence's behalf. Madam Fauveau might have an argument to say she didn't even know that these documents were going to be used at all at the point that she had completed her cross-examination, but she's quite capable of making that submission herself in due course, but we do submit that really this is an improper use of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can assure Mr. Josse, Mr. President, that the Prosecution does not view this as a game. And I think, after a year together, you know how many times I've stood up and said no questions on redirect. It's been the vast majority. But as I heard the cross-examination, as you know, I did not ask this witness probably for obvious reasons to go into the definition of Mr. Miletic's job or General Gvero's job. That was not the purpose of my direct. You saw the purpose of my direct. Mr. Gvero and Mr. Miletic had this witness talk about their job. I seem to remember that my memorable about Miletic is that he's the mailman, he opens mail, and that's all he does. This witness talked briefly about General Gvero issuing I think press releases and then his last few statements is that despite working with him for several years, he doesn't have any idea of what he does and knows nothing about it. And so this opens a door. This is not something I went in on direct. They are basically as we could see went beyond the scope of the -- of my -- sorry, they went beyond the scope of the examination, which is their right. It's not something I object to because we don't want to have to call the witness back but they went beyond the scope. They went into the definition of the job. Basically described the job as he did in those terms and one of his big jobs was creating a chess board. So they have opened the door. I spent a good part of yesterday, you know, identifying key issues related to the job definition so that I could put those before you and ask this professional officer to comment on them briefly. They opened that door wide open. It's not one I intended to get into with this witness but now that it's open I would like to have the chance to be able to do it. I'm relying on your previous ruling that some documents don't necessarily have to have a 65 ter number. We've looked at these documents, they've all been provided to the Defence. Some of them do not have 65 ter numbers. We found some of them relatively recently and they've either been given to the Defence and then put on our next motion for 65 ter numbers or sometimes we e-mailed the Defence saying look we found one that doesn't. But we know what your ruling has been regarding the redirect. This allegation that this is somehow I'm improperly trying to slide documents in is just inappropriate and unnecessary. I'm not trying to play a game with you to do this. I would prefer to sit down and let Mr. Vanderpuye go to work but these doors have been wide open and Miletic's door is that the witness also stated that he didn't -- the Main Staff didn't know anything about the Srebrenica operation until it happened. Now, that's -- wasn't the Prosecution's position to give the Court a blow by blow of every time the Main Staff may have heard information about the Srebrenica operation. As you saw, I stuck with the 12, the 13th of July and the Main Staff's direct involvement in the crimes of this case. But now that they've had this witness say, "All of us in the Main Staff" and he was talking for all of them, "We didn't know anything about the Srebrenica operation." So I've got a few documents, some have 65 ter, some don't, that shed light on this issue when the Main Staff became aware of various aspects of the Srebrenica operation. I won't -- you know me, I'm not a real talker if I can help it, and I hope to do this relatively quickly and the reason I was talking that first document is to make him comfortable, give him a chance to look at it and then go over the key parts of it so that's the Prosecution's position on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Madam Fauveau, I also noticed your client has been standing wishing to tell us something. Do you wish to go first?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I would like to ask for your leave to let me speak first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please, you want to speak first, so General, could you sit down, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't intend to speak at great length, but I suppose do I have the right to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will, but first I'm giving the floor to your lawyer and then you will have your chance so please sit down and Madam Fauveau will say what she needs to say. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I would like to say that we never advanced the theory that Mr. Miletic was a mailman and more importantly, the position, the tasks and the duties and functions of General Miletic are at the very heart of the Prosecution case. It has been challenged from the beginning. So the Prosecutor cannot say that we now have a witness who we have in front of us who is from the Main Staff is somebody we will not deal with seriously. He asked himself about that, as for knowledge about Srebrenica, what the Defence did was to respond to issues that were raised by the Prosecution in their examination-in-chief. Moreover, we explicitly relied on the witness's evidence. So I believe it is completely inappropriate to say that it was the cross-examination that opened the door into some completely new matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to use the words of the gentleman across this room. I would like, though, to be able to attend this trial without being insulted. I don't know what education this gentleman has received, but from what he says, I can see how much he knows. I would appreciate it if he could refrain from insulting me as a person. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And General Miletic, it's not my intention to ever insult this -- any of the accused. I don't take this personal. I was paraphrasing the answer of the Colonel when he talked about opening the mail and he didn't -- he didn't have much authority to do anything but opening the mail, something to that effect. That's my paraphrase. If it's a little rough, I apologise, but that was fundamentally what he said in answer to some question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A brief right to reply if I may to what Mr. McCloskey said in response to my submissions. We contend that the questions that Mr. Krgovic asked were basically those the witness had been asked in the course of his interview. For the most part Mr. Krgovic directed the witness to the interview. Of note, though this doesn't come out in the course of cross-examination, I'm sure it won't be disputed, the document that he cross-examined on today, P45, a document of some importance in the case of General Gvero, the witness was asked about in the course of his interview, unlike the vast swathe of documents that appear on the list that we have received today. And to that extent, we submit that there is a real difference between the questions Mr. Krgovic asked and those that my learned friend proposes now to ask. Finally, could I endorse what Madam Fauveau has just said? The questions that Mr. Krgovic asked of this witness are fundamental to the defence of my client. Yes, it may be that there is a certain amount of humour in relation to the chess document. But basically, the thrust of that cross-examination is identical to the case that we have advanced throughout this case. It doesn't take my learned friend by surprise at all. He chose to call Colonel Trkulja. This ultimately is a trial being run on traditional common law grounds; to this extent, if he chooses to call him, then he's by the rules of examination, cross-examination and re-examination, and he can't, in effect, seek to cross-examine the witness with this vast array of documents. So for these various reasons we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Briefly. This is precisely why I need to get into the real definition of this job. We've talked about chess, we've talked about other light weight issues associated with General Gvero's job. And I won't repeat some of what he said about General Gvero's knowledge and what he said about his lack of ability. But this document is the job. It's the reality of the job, and it was not something I wanted to get into, but when they take a Prosecution witness down that road and concentrate on you suggesting he's dealing with chess, he's dealing with other issues that are not substantive and they don't get into any of the substantive issues, the propaganda issues, the dealings with the international community issues, it's incumbent upon me, important that I get you back to the issues of the case with this witness. And that's the only reason why I've done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to intervene at the appropriate time concerning the Court's ruling concerning the use of documents which are not on the Rule 65 ter list and maybe that it is the right time to do it now, given that the witness is already outside. It's with your leave, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not open for discussion. That has been decided. We have handed down a ruling on that. And we don't want to hear further submissions on the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's bring -- wait before we bring in the witness. We need to discuss a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I notice General --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, just a few words. I have the impression, with all due respect to the Prosecutor and Your Honours, that it is necessary to say the following: This document which would have been introduced sooner or later about the duties and responsibilities of the organ for morale, religious and legal affairs has been introduced without any connection with examination-in-chief. Apart from that, my Defence team has had no opportunity to consult me about it and professionally speaking, they are ignorant of many important things in that area. Therefore, I believe it is inappropriate to introduce such sensitive documentation and argument in this way. In addition to that, out of seven pages of this document, the Prosecutor invokes only one little bit on the penultimate page. That little bit, Your Honours, requires a lot of knowledge about the methodology of work in order to be grasped properly and explained. Done this way, it will be introduced into the debate on the subject in a very inadequate way. I don't mind having it discussed, but I do mind its introduction in this way, which might lead to inappropriate conclusions being made later. Speaking of this material, there is a lot of evidence that concerning the operation Srebrenica, some other superior commander took responsibility for propaganda and similar activities, which shows that it was outside my purview. I can perhaps even point you to the page. I would like the Court to understand it properly and I do object to having documents introduced in this way, if they are crucial for proper understanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Gvero. I suppose the best policy would be to allow your counsel to raise the appropriate objections at the right time rather than intervene at times only to prove the need for some further questions to be put on the issue. However, you have made one point that is definitely important, and I will say it subject to agreement by my colleagues, namely that if you feel that you require some time to consult with your counsel on this document, the reason being that you have not been given the opportunity to discuss it with them, you will be allowed the appropriate time and opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just it may be helpful. This has been on the 65 ter list since December 6, 2006 and your ruling, so it's not a new document but I do think the general is correct, he should be able to talk with his counsel about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Josse, do you also wish to have a chance to consult with your client on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have the break very soon so that you will have the opportunity to consult, but before we do so, we will hand down our ruling on the points raised by you, Mr. Josse. In relation -- this applies only in relation to the points raised by you. They do not necessarily apply to the points raised by you, Ms. Fauveau. We'll come to that later on, if there is an objection, an ad hoc objection. The position is you're right, Mr. Josse, in suggesting that Colonel Trkulja should have an opportunity, full opportunity, to read the entire document before he is asked any questions on it, in whole or in part. Second point we wish to rule about is that we have followed both the examination-in-chief and the cross -- and your cross-examination, or that of Mr. Krgovic, and both during cross-examination and during the testimony of Mr. Trkulja on cross-examination, the qualifications, role, functions and activities of General Gvero came to highlight, and in view of that, we have no doubt in our mind that the Prosecution has a right on re-examination to go into these issues and for that purpose to use the document that we have in front of us. So we'll have a break now, instead of having the break at quarter to 4.00, we are having it now. That will give you, Ms. Fauveau as well, the opportunity to consult with your client, and you Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Josse, I don't know, or anyone else, for that matter, to consult with your clients. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, let me make it clear that we are not seeking to go behind the ruling that the Chamber has already made. But bearing in mind the Chamber kindly allowed us to see our client. Following that consultation, we have one further submission, and it's this: We would invite the Chamber to instruct the Prosecution to ask the witness in relation to each and every document whether the witness has previously seen the document, and if so, in what context. In other words, at the time of these events or subsequently in an interview or in a proofing session. If the witness says that he has never seen the document, then we do ask rhetorically on what basis the witness is being asked about the document. If it's as an expert, then we invite the Chamber to consider whether he is a suitable and appropriate expert bearing in mind his expertise appears to be tanks and armoured mechanical vehicles in general. If it's not as an expert, then we ask on what basis is he being asked these questions? Those are our further submissions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I would object to being ordered on which questions to ask. In particular, it's the concepts that this document sets forth that I'm most interested in and it's only in response to what the Court very clearly said, that Defence got into on cross-examination the job description, the duties, the authority of this position. Those are the concepts in this document that I'm interested in asking this witness about. I will probably, just because it's a Main Staff document and something he may have seen, you know, ask that question and I should. But it's not as counsel wishes as a foundation not to ask any more. I think I can ask him about the concepts in this document: Does he know that, for example, General Gvero takes part in talking to international agencies? Does he know General Gvero has close contact with intelligence and security organs, as this thing says? This kind of thing, I should be able to do and based as the material that's in the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number 1, we are all here used to systems whereby it's -- usually the Judge doesn't tell the parties what questions or what procedure to follow. In any case, our position is that without telling you what to do and what not to do at this stage, Mr. McCloskey, I think the point made by Mr. Josse, namely that the Trial Chamber should have before it knowledge as to whether a particular document has -- is already known to the witness is an important matter, and, again, I think we should know that -- get that information in relation to each document that you will be putting to the witness. Second thing raised by -- second matter raised by Mr. Josse, I think, doesn't deserve much more comment than what I'm going to say, namely that at no point have we had an indication that this witness was being dealt with either by the Prosecution or a by the Defence as an expert. Our question is if according, as you said, Mr. Josse, he is only knowledgeable about the particular division that he was in charge of, why on earth ask him so many questions in the first place on the role of a general or assistant commander. But in any case, what we have decided is that at the end, if when Mr. McCloskey has finished, if you show cause why you should put further questions to the witness on re-cross, we will consider allowing that, depending on circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So are we ready to bring in the witness? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other thing I forgot to mention that obviously if it's the case of a document that needs going through on the part of the witness, we will, of course, allow that. Colonel, we are back. We have discussed what we needed to discuss and I think Mr. McCloskey is now in a position to proceed with his redirect. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have completed command staff academy. The documents that were drafted, Gvero and some of his assistants completed political schools, and they were familiar with this. The school that I finished doesn't teach you to draft documents like the one I have before me. When it comes to such documents, I am a layperson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that information. And thank you also for your patience, Colonel. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And thank you, Colonel. I notice you brought the document back. Did you have a -- sorry for having you work at the break but did you have a chance to review it so that you were -- at least have a chance to review it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I don't intend to get into technical details with you about this job but I just wanted to ask you a few questions. Do you remember having seen this document ever before?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I just -- under the title, "Within psychological and propaganda activities," I just want to ask you, did you know that one of General Gvero's job was to take part in propaganda?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of some things only superficially. All this was part of his sector, and I'm not able to provide you any more details because all that would be merely a guessing game and it would be beside the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We don't need to get into details but I'm just trying to see if some of these points in the document are something you had any knowledge about. So you do have some knowledge that this propaganda was part of his job, I guess. Then let me ask you about -- it's right under propaganda. It says, "Realise tight cooperation with intelligence, security and other organs of the command in order to exchange" -- is the proper English translation that I'm agreed upon with counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Exchange information and mutual coordination of measures, activities and behaviour." So did have you any knowledge as part of General Gvero's job, he should have a tight cooperation with the intelligence and security organs?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's not something you heard about. All right. Let's go to this last section. It's entitled, "Other social subjects such as international organisations and institutions." Do you see that? It's within paragraph 3 of the document, right before paragraph 4, entitled, "Legal affairs." Do you see the legal affairs section there at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just look up right above legal affairs is the section I'm talking about and it's a simple question: This document says that it's part of the job to, in section D, cooperate with the Red Cross organisation, Commission for Refugees, and other humanitarian organisations in order to resolve living problems of soldiers and their families. Did you know that that was part of his job, General Gvero's?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I never discussed things with Gvero and his assistant Sokanovic and others. I never asked them what their competences were, what they were authorised to do, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But this -- it says helping resolve the living problems of soldiers and their families. You must have known if General Gvero was helping soldiers in issues of morale and with all the tragedies of war. Don't you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Must have known sounds very much like a leading question, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you ought to rephrase the question, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never took any of their documents in my hands, I never read any of them. And in conversations, well...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the other one. It says, "F, cooperate with UNPROFOR and international humanitarian organisations according to the views, instructions and orders of the superior commands." Did you know -- and I say especially at the time of Srebrenica -- that General Gvero -- or whether or not General Gvero was speaking to UNPROFOR commanders, was speaking to UNPROFOR representatives?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. General Gvero was the commander's assistant and I could see him only if I was invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Didn't you say he had something to do with press reports or issuing press statements?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must have had, because nobody else was designated to do those things, and in any case, all that fell under the larger or broader area of morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, on that issue of dealing with the press or the international organisations, do you remember back in around the time that Srebrenica fell, 11 through about 17 of July, General Gvero getting in a big disagreement or problem with President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask to you take that look at a document, and it's number 2756, and I'll give you a copy in Serbian. I think I've given you the right one. And take your time to take a look at it. It's dated 17 July. It's to the Main Staff of the VRS, General Gvero, assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs personally, dated 17 July 1995. And we see that's from the president of the republic and the Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska armed forces, Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It begins --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clear the issue whether he's seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard about this obvious -- well, what I believe is obvious, an obvious, serious disagreement between the president and General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of General Gvero sabotaging --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Better let me finish, because I don't want to suggest General Gvero sabotaging as a saboteur. Let me finish. Did he sabotage any order of President Karadzic pertaining to the information ministry's exclusive task of information?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't a clue. At the command post, we never discussed such things. We never went into the details of relation -- the relationship between Gvero and others. No, we never discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So none of these things that the president is accusing General Gvero of, had you heard about?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this could have only been discussed in the inner circle of the command. When it comes to the broader circle...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your experience, you don't think this kind of a conflict might find its way out into officers such as yourself that are down in the bunker with these guys?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I have General Gvero's response to this, which, given the answers to the questions, I won't ask him about unless counsel wants or the Court would like to see it. Okay. All right. There is a -- I now would like to go to this document, it's number 45, it's the 13 July order in the name of General Gvero that counsel spoke briefly about, you and I had spoke briefly about it. I think you have established on cross-examination that General Gvero did not actually type this or draft this order and that it came out of the operations unit. How do you know it -- from those numbers that it came out of the operations unit?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was recorded by the operative officer and I'm reading the number here, 03/4-1629. That's how it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do we know that's the operative organ? Is that their number or --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe that you will find that number in their registry book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who do you think would have actually drafted this order for the signature of General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it would have been Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to call your attention to the first paragraph, and I'm going to ask you about -- you said -- it says based on instructions received. So clearly those, as I think you've stated, those -- this -- the information in this document came from instructions from somewhere else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again where do you -- if -- where would you think those instructions would have come from?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- these pieces of information or instruction could have only come from the commander. Nobody else had the right to order something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Once this document goes down under General Gvero's name, is he responsible for it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person responsible is the person who provided the instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But if a senior officer passes on an order, is that senior officer that knowingly passes on an order also responsible for it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every document, every order, has the introductory part which connects that order to a certain person or to a certain previous order. Here, this document is connected. It is linked to a person, to a figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course it is, as are most orders, but what I'm asking is when a senior officer like General Gvero gets this kind of information, signs off for it and passes it throughout the VRS, is he now in part responsible for the order?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Because of the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if General Mladic issues an illegal order to someone in the Main Staff and that Main Staff person passes it on to the corps and that corps person passes it on to the brigade and that brigade person passes it on to the battalion and that battalion person passes it on to the other organs, General Mladic is the only one that's responsible; is that correct? Is that what you're saying? Or is general -- excuse me, is General Mladic the only one responsible?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish what you had to say, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If something is illegal, if it's against the state, against its people, then the first person in line who receives that illegal order is not duty-bound to carry that order out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Our submission was that that question, A, calls for speculation, and/or in effect went to the realm of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't agree with you. I think the witness is being asked questions which are within his knowledge. If he knows, he knows. If he doesn't know, if he can't answer, he's free to tell us, "I don't know." Let's proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, I understand your answer that an officer receiving an illegal order is not duty-bound to follow it. But if he passes that order on in the chain that I discussed, is he in part responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have exhausted this area. Let's move on to a different question, Mr. McCloskey. He's answered you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in the first paragraph of this order, it says, "Based on instructions received, and following defeat in the Srebrenica enclave, the men from the enclave fit for military service were tasked with crossing over to Tuzla and Kladanj in groups and carrying weapons. Among them are inveterate criminals and villains who will stop at nothing just to avoid being captured and reach Muslim-controlled territory." Were you aware at the time on July 13th, that General Mladic or General Gvero were referring to the Muslim men and civilians as inveterate criminals and villains?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this how you believe the Main Staff viewed the Muslims at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there is another order there, and there is another order involving 5.000 people who passed through. This is all speculation. This is all -- one still didn't know how big the convoy was, where it was headed to, what it was up to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Colonel. I'd like to ask you if you have knowledge of another document, and that's document 131. And I can show you, there is an original, looks like a -- well, a typed version. I don't know about original. And then there is a handwritten version as well. Go ahead and take a look at it. This one is from General Tolimir. It's 13 July. On 13 July, were you personally aware -- I'm sorry, let me know once you've had a chance to finish.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I've finished. I finished reading. This was never read at the Main Staff. This is the first time I see this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about the information in it? Let me ask you a couple of questions. Were you aware about hundreds of prisoners from Srebrenica on 13 -- in the custody of the VRS on 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that nobody at the command post was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the first PO, PBR, in Semec [phoen], what does that mean? Petrinja light infantry brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an infantry brigade but I don't know what the other letters stand for. It could be their location where they were deployed, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember which brigade this is. But it is an infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know of any reason why such a group of people could be used for agricultural work in that area and why they would need to be transported at night and not be in contact with other prisoners? Any idea about this?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any idea why this would be sent to General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you testified on cross-examination, you stated that the Main Staff didn't know about the operation against Srebrenica until reports started coming in. Can you clarify that for us? When do you believe the Main Staff first became aware of the July operation to take down Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the reports started coming in, but even then we didn't know which forces, where, how they are advancing. In fact, we didn't know which forces were taking part in the Srebrenica operation or the losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say when the reports started coming in, what do you mean? What, roughly, when did reports start coming in?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they started coming in as the units started advancing, conquering one part of the territory after another, until final liberation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if I can tell you historically, the first big movement was July 6th, do you know how many -- roughly how many days prior to July 6th you would have gotten information about this operation, the Main Staff and yourself, that is?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau? One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe this is speculation. If the Prosecutor wants to show the report to the witness, I have nothing against it, but how can he ask how many days before the 6th if the witness doesn't even know that there was something on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was assuming the witness, since he described the movements of the troops, that if he could just start from the part where he was aware of the movement of the troops, just roughly how long before the movement of the troops did he get reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he obviously doesn't know. So let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any idea? I mean a month? I mean, it would make a big difference on how many documents I show him is why. A month before the operation started? A week before? Can you give us your best -- don't guess but if you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that again is speculation because the Prosecutor himself uses the word "guess." I don't see the purpose of such evidence even if given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the Prosecutor has done precisely tried to avoid what you objected to. He's telling the witness straight and plain that he is not to speculate, he is not to guess. If he knows, he knows, if he doesn't, he will tell us that he doesn't. So let's move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's see if we can go over some documents and perhaps this will refresh your recollection about when the Main Staff would have been aware of the attack on Srebrenica. Let's go to a document that was, I believe, discussed briefly with you by counsel. It's known to us as directive 7. You talked about it a bit and I've got a -- P00005. I've got it and I think I've marked it under the section of Drina Corps. You've talked about this a bit already. And if you could just read that paragraph about the Drina Corps, it's pretty short. Do you see Drina Corps mentioned there? I think if you go to that red tab, it should be the Drina Corps section but feel free to look at the entire document, of course, if you need to. Okay. And I won't read that whole section, but it -- as you've just read, it does say, and this as we know is an order or a directive from President Karadzic, "While in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible." It says a bit more. And then it says, "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations." And then it talks about the objective which I don't think I need to go over. It's at English page 10, B/C/S page 15. Is this an order from President Karadzic to develop a plan as soon as possible to separate the enclaves and such?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably it is, but there is no date here to indicate when it would have been drafted, and he didn't -- he gave names to individual operations, so it's absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And, well, in your experience, when the president says, "Get an operation going as soon as possible," can you give us an idea of militarily how the generals respond to that? Is it something they just can forget about or is it something that they would act on? If you can answer.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only tell you on the basis of my experience, although I was not present in this specific case when this was read or processed and worked on, but based on my experience, whatever the commander, supreme commander, orders has to be executed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this an order that you were aware of, this directive?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single organ of the branches of service was familiar with this directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, there is -- and I won't get into it but in paragraph 6 of this, on English 14, under support for combat operations, there is a whole section on morale and psychological support. And I would guess that with all these activities, that armour would be something that would be a consideration as well. But given that, I understand your answer. Do you want to change it after taking a look at -- your answer about not a single organ was mentioned to this?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I meant organs of the staff, chiefs of engineering, artillery, et cetera. I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just -- just to go on briefly a little bit under that Drina Corps section, it also talks about, in the next paragraph, that in case the UNPROFOR forces leave Zepa and Srebrenica, the Drina Corps command shall plan an operation named Jadar with the task of breaking up and destroying the Muslim forces in these enclaves and definitively liberating the Drina valley region. Were you aware of that part of that, that they not only wanted to separate the enclaves but if UNPROFOR left, actually to take the enclaves and liberate them completely?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given you an answer. I was not familiar with the entirety of this directive. That means this, what follows, and everything till the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says here that the planning of this operation shall be the responsibility of the Drina Corps command. In planning an operation of this sort, would the Drina Corps communicate its plans with the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, the instruction for the work of command staff, any plan made by a subordinate unit is submitted to the commander for signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if the Prosecutor could tell us exactly which passage he read, because in this passage, we see references to at least three operations. I would like to know to which operation this particular sentence applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before he does that, on a logistical matter, Your Honour, I don't think the screen is changing the text. So I suspect the accused are unable to follow this cross-examination. Certainly, it hasn't changed for the last few minutes. So I think the operator, and I can understand this, is having difficulty keeping up with the cross-examination, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both. Let's attend first to the matter raised by Mr. Josse. I am not in a position to know, because I don't understand the language, especially if it's in Serbian. What page are we on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the Drina Corps is the second half of the page, isn't it? Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This section that I'm talking about is just a few short paragraphs, and my question was a general one. It was when the -- what was my question? When the corps is planning an operation would they normally communicate or coordinate with the Main Staff, an operation, any operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's be specific first in relation to the paragraph that you were referring the witness to, because apparently, as I understood, there are several paragraphs relating to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think he's able to follow me. It starts with -- it's page 11 in the English. It's the third paragraph down. In the B/C/S it would be the fourth paragraph. In the Serbian it should be the fourth paragraph under the Drina Corps section. And it just says "Planning and execution of combat actions in both operations shall be the responsibility of the Drina Corps command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, and that goes on, this appears [In English] to be executed after the end of the Spreca 95 operation and before Prozor 95. [Interpretation] So the only thing I want to know is what is the link between these operations and the Krivaja operation, which is our only concern here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey? I think I can identify in Cyrillic now the paragraph that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All I'm doing is asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I can't help you more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It wasn't my intention to get into too much detail about these other operations. I can a little bit but -- and I will, if that will help counsel, but I would like first to get my -- see if I can get an answer from my question that when you see an order or when the main -- when the corps is designated to plan an operation, would they normally work or coordinate or communicate with the Main Staff? This of course is central to the theme of redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, does that make sense? I'm sorry to -- sometimes we take a while to get a question out.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
