utterances.text: There is some sense but believe me, after the operation, they didn't bring any documentation to the Main Staff so that the entire Main Staff could review it, so I cannot give you an answer as to whether they brought anything, when, or how. I told you I didn't know anything about Krivaja and the other operations which were never carried out any way, until the reports started coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Were you -- did you take any part or did you get any assignment in this operation that's the next one down? Let me just keep reading from where I left off. "By the end of March, an agreement with the east Bosnia corps command, take part in the planning of Spreca 95 operation, which has the task of cutting off the Muslim armed forces along the Kalesija-Simin Han line and then breaking them up and destroying them in the region of Teocak, Sapna and Vitinica, thus finally removing the danger of a Muslim breakthrough towards the Drina north of Zvornik." Do you remember taking part or helping out in any way in that, in Spreca 95, as it's described in this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have to cast my mind back a little. I don't know what operation that was. I know I helped a tank company from the Protection Regiment to be transferred to that area somewhere. Whether it was Spreca or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness said something at the end that sounded vaguely like, "But it didn't work."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this what you wanted to refer to, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't successful, he exactly said something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree to that, Colonel? In other words, that when you were answering the last question, you said, whether it was Spreca or not, I don't know, did you add something about this operation being successful or not successful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, were you -- did you hear any information about a planned attack by the Drina Corps around the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, planned for 15 May 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you hear, you at the Main Staff? I take it you were at the Main Staff in May of -- April, May of 1995. Did you hear about any plan to attack the enclave in order to set up a further attack on the enclaves? Anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you can look at another document, it's number 204. It's a -- and I'll give you the original we have or a -- excuse me, a Serbian of it. And again take -- you can take your time. I'm not going to get into a lot of details with you on this but if you could -- it's a good idea to see if this refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your remembrance of the tank in the Spreca operation gave me some confidence you might be able to remember some things. We can see in this document, which is dated 15 May 1995, that General Krstic -- excuse me. It says Colonel Krstic at the time, as the deputy commander of the Drina Corps, is ordering -- you can see it on page 2 of the English -- "I order as soon as possible, using the neighbouring forces around the Zepa enclaves," and it goes on and talks about the Zepa enclave, the Srebrenica enclave and various forces, and an offensive operation. And if you look at it, interestingly enough, on -- under paragraph 3.1, page 3 of 5 in the English, and scattered throughout this document are references to the 65th ZMTP company. Is that the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is the 65th Protection Regiment a unit of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is also a reference to the 67th -- I think it's Communications Regiment. Is that a unit of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 67th Communications Regiment, yes. It's a unit of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have any recollection of General Krstic working closely, involving units of the Main Staff in this operation? Any recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness answered, but if he could say whether he remembers this document, if he had seen it before, and if he remembers this particular operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm trying my best to ask the questions, Mr. President. I don't understand -- I think I'm asking him if he has any memory of this operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From his answer, which was a no, to your question, he doesn't seem to have that he has any recollection at all, but again, that was limited to the question that you put. So what Mrs. Fauveau has raised is whether he remembers this document. I think we have an indication that he doesn't, but I don't want to steal words from him. Perhaps we can ask the questions ourselves, Mr. McCloskey, and make it easier on you. Colonel, did you ever see this document before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you remember the particular operation that General Krstic refers to in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can leave it at that and proceed to the next question, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you now to go to a document -- this is document 9398, dated the same date, 16 May 1995. 2892 is the number. And this is a combat report from the Drina Corps to the Main Staff. It's the kind of document that you received in assembling the Main Staff reports. And there is a paragraph in this that I -- I don't have an English translation but if you could read this paragraph for us, it's paragraph 8, actually, if we could scroll to paragraph 8, let me give this to you so you can -- you can read it, the whole thing. But you can take a look at the whole document.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, this document did not reach -- look at the heading -- did not reach Crna Rijeka, nor the place where the commander was in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, it's written to the Main Staff of the VRS, IKM 1, Main Staff of the VRS, Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the IKM of the Main Staff doing in Zvornik on May 15th, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the commander was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, wouldn't a copy of that been sent on to Crna Rijeka as well?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have been written among the addressees. You see there is only one copy addressed to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you -- and I'm sorry, I don't have an English, but could you look at that paragraph 8? It's the second paragraph. It starts with odluka. Could you help us and slowly read that? It's really the second half of that little paragraph I'm interested in, but could you read that entire paragraph starting with odluka slowly so that we can see what it says? And I'm sorry, out loud because that's the only way that we are going to understand it, for those of us that don't understand Serbian.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the western part of the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't need that paragraph. It's just the second one, beginning --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Odluka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- odluka, yes. And remember go slow because they are translating you.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. "Decision. With the forces in the western part of the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, defend decisively the defence lines reached or attained. Whereas the interspace of Zepa and Srebrenica should be controlled by sending strong reconnaissance groups, one platoon strong, or a company strong, with the purpose of locating and neutralising enemy reconnaissance groups and their combat support, and thus prevent communication between enclaves. Continue preparations for closing the enclaves completely and use the available forces of the MUP in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps to control the territory behind the lines in depth. Continue to carry out the Spreca 95 operation in keeping with the decision of the Main Staff of the VRS. Deputy commander, Colonel Radislav Krstic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. What I want to ask you about is that section that says, "Continue the preparations for closing the enclaves completely." This statement, "Continue the preparations for closing the enclaves," suggests -- appears to suggest -- and tell me if I'm wrong -- that the receiver of this information would know what they were -- what they meant by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can ask it in a different way to--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But let's hear the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's a question that really should have been asked in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse, and please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this document appear to you, this statement appear to you, to suggest prior knowledge of the person that receives it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same objection. Why doesn't my learned friend ask what does it suggest to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the same. I think you have read out the corresponding part of the paragraph. Just ask him what he understands by it. What does he understand by "continue the preparations"? What does he understand by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not a question I wanted to ask. That will get a whole new answer that I'm not interested in but I--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let's move on to the next question, if you don't want to ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were at the Main Staff. Do you know what this statement means?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The statement that "continue preparations for the separation of the enclaves."

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means that the enclaves were not separated and there was normal communication between Zepa and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. In your experience in receiving these kinds of reports from the corps -- oh, I think I'll go on, Mr. President. I apologise. Let's go to a -- let's go to the Main Staff, the document from the Main Staff to the Presidency for 16 May. And I'd like you to -- and that is -- I'll have a number for you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I may be wrong but that was 2892, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll have a number for you in a minute but it's a Main Staff report to the president dated 16 May 1995, it's ERN 04261017. And I may have left this off the list. I apologise. But there is a reference that I just need you to read for us, if you could. It's paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not objecting in advance that this document be shown to the witness but we have no idea what is in it. We've never seen it. Maybe it wasn't even disclosed to us. It's not on the 65 ter list. It's not on this list here. So maybe the Prosecutor can continue his re-examination otherwise and then during the break we can see what this is about and maybe the question can be put later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can find out -- find that out immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is not a mystery document. It's just one of the many reports from the Main Staff to the Presidency which counsel has a full collection of. This is redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's beside the point, whether it's in redirect or not. The thing is that everyone is being taken by surprise as to the contents of this document. So if we could see it on the screen, give everyone the opportunity to read it and know what we are talking about. This is basically the gist of it. She is not objecting as such prematurely, at least, or peremptorily to the use of this document for the time being but we -- even we need to know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. I'm getting there, trying. If it gets put on the ELMO and read by him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Two lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could show him the part that's highlighted? Could you put it on the ELMO? And I'm sorry about this awkwardness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau? While the witness is reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask leave of the Court to have physical opportunity to see the first and the last page of this document before the witness starts to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, are there any other documents that are not listed in the list that was circulated today? The last list, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I may have made another mistake. I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what we are going to do is this -- instead of having the break when I was told we should have it, that's at 5.30, we will have it now. On your part, please try to find out if there are any other such documents that are going to emerge that the Defence have not been alerted to and in the meantime you will have an opportunity to examine these documents. So instead of having the break at 5.30, we will have it now and it will be the usual 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope the Chamber don't regard this as a very pedantic point but it's a matter of some concern to a number of Defence counsel and I can say at least more than one of the accused. I did mention it briefly to Mr. McCloskey and he has an explanation. Could we quickly get P45 up on e-court? Because we'll need it for the point that I'm going to make. While that is being done could I invite the Chamber to turn to page 38 of the transcript of today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At line -- at line 8 to 9, Mr. McCloskey ended a quote with a question, "Were you aware at the time, on July 13th, that General Mladic or General Gvero, referring to the Muslim men and civilians as inveterate criminals and villains?" The actual document, P45 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does not mention civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- doesn't mention civilians. It also uses the words "among them." Those were the two points. I hope that, as I say, the Chamber doesn't regard that as too pedantic. I accept that Mr. McCloskey has said to me that in effect it was a question he was asking the witness but from our point of view it's extremely material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a valid point you have raised. You're definitely not being pedantic, Mr. Josse. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was a deliberate question. I was not trying to rephrase the document. I was referring to what I believe was an established fact in this case that I don't believe counsel is objecting to or is fighting, I'd like to know if they are, and that was merely that there were civilians in this group, so my question had to do with did they have knowledge or did they -- did you know about the column and the civilians. I wasn't trying to just rehash the document. That's not what I was doing. I was using the document to make my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But let's -- your question was phrased as follows: "Were you aware at the time on July 13th that General Mladic and General Gvero were referring to the Muslim men and civilians as inveterate criminals and villians?" If you look at the respective paragraph on P45, it says: "Based on the instructions received and following defeat in the Srebrenica enclave, the men from the enclave fit for military service were tasked with crossing over to Tuzla and Kladanj in groups and carrying weapons. Amongst them" -- that is, amongst these names -- these men, "are inveterate criminals and villains who will stop at nothing just to avoid being captured and reach Muslim-controlled territories." This is what the paragraph says. The objection is that when you read this paragraph from P45, although it may be referring also to civilians being amongst the group that were crossing over, allegedly crossing over to Tuzla, the attribution of inveterate criminals and villains, this is Mr. Josse's suggestion, is not referring to them but it's referring to those who are not civilians. This is as I understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I suppose what I was saying is the question mischaracterised the evidence, i.e. the document. Mr. McCloskey says that it was in the form of a question, well, in which case, it could arguably be said to be a leading question. That doesn't really matter. It's more a point of information that we were very anxious was put on the record. I'm not asking my learned friend to go back and put it right with the witness. We were simply very anxious, I repeat, to put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have taken both points and we can leave it at that. According to you, when you have a description of men from the enclave fit for military service, it includes civilians as well, and therefore the inveterate criminals and villains could be amongst them too. This is what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Precisely correct, Your Honour, as an established fact in the case, not mischaracterising any evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. That's -- what he is alleging to be mischaracterising is not the Colonel's evidence but the document. This is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand it and I'm saying I wasn't trying to mess with the document. I was just using it to make my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But I think we have -- it's good on your part to have raised it because we will know what your position is at least and for you to have clarified the reason why you put or you phrased the question you way you did. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you both. Can we bring the witness in? Can I get you together, try to finish with this witness today, please? Mr. McCloskey, how much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sensing I'm -- I should be finishing up, but this door has been opened so wide on this issue that it's hard for me to step away from it, and I do have one more topic I'm going to get into, but I'm not going to get into any documents in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's see what happens. Is the other witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel, thank you, we've got the document up on the screen. And basically what I was trying to do, this is the Main Staff document going to the president, and we had already seen the corps document coming to the Main Staff, and could you just read out this section B including this part that's highlighted, just in my -- just to see if there is any connection between the part that was in the document from the corps and this part that's been put in the Main Staff document to the Presidency? So if could you start with section B, there, stanje u korpusu?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Situation in the corps. All corps units are under full combat readiness. They are successfully holding the lines reached. Preparations continue to stabilise the defence around the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. In the course of the day, the 1st Vlasenica infantry brigade carried out reconnoitring and scoured the terrain on the Libina-Glogic axis. It was noticed that an enemy group had stayed in the aforementioned sector. During the course of the day tomorrow, the 1st Vlasenica Infantry Brigade will continue scouring the ground. C, losses: There were no losses." This was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And from what you remember of the communication from the corps on this subject of Srebrenica, does this brief reference to Srebrenica and enclaves appear to be -- to you to be taken from the Drina Corps report which would of course indicate that somebody from the Main Staff would have read that report? Or can you tell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was taken -- look here. I drafted very many of these reports. I often drafted them. And whatever was included for any of the corps was actually taken from that particular corps report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you a map to see if you have any familiarity with it, to see if you remember the name of this potential operation that may or may not have been known to some people. And it's number 2885. I don't intend to spend a lot of time with it but the main thing is the -- and if I could get some help from the usher just to show you this map, show the parts of it, Your Honour, Mr. President, are on the computer, but the computer isn't much good for these sorts of things. Can you take a -- just take a look at this original map, Colonel? And I can just help, I think, the Court and the people to understand just some of the basics that it said but in the right-hand corner it says military secret, strictly confidential, Susica and then on the other side it says approved by commander General Ratko Mladic. And in the middle it says, battle plan of the Drina Corps command. And then Susica, I believe, something to that effect. But there aren't any signatures or stamps or anything on this document or dates, are there, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we ask how this arises from cross-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've been asking the witness -- this -- well, this explanation should probably not be done in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can you ask the witness, please -- Witness, can you remove your headphones, please? Let's hear the explanation. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've been asking the witness, Your Honour, about the May 15th battle plan of General Krstic's directed towards the enclave that we went over briefly, and he did not have any information or knowledge about it. I'm continuing to see if he will remember this operation. This map, the only thing I have with operation Susica on it is this map, and this map, it's in the position of the Prosecution is very similar to the attack plan that is outlined by General Krstic in the May 15th document that I asked the witness about. So this is further attempt to see if he remembers the name of this operation and he can also tell us, we have General Mladic's name on this thing, and of course he's a member of the Main Staff, and the issues here is does the Main Staff know about the operations. That's why I'm asking him is it signed? It's not signed which will be an indication that perhaps General Mladic doesn't -- or didn't have this in his hands. But that's what this is all about. It's the topic of does the Main Staff know about these operations, does he remember anything, can he remember anything? And I can tell you, he remembered something about operation Spreca, which is -- was giving me some hope. I'm not just using him as a back-stop although I clearly am using him to respond to what the Defence said, even though his memory doesn't seem to be so good. But I've got one more area after this and I'll be wrapping it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We maintain our objection. Your Honours I think have ruled in relation to my objection to this amounts to cross-examination, but in reality, what my learned friend says shows that really it is cross-examination rather than re-examination. But on the separate ground, it really is a separate ground, we say this is simply a step too far and it doesn't arise from anything either my learned friend Madam Fauveau asked or we asked on behalf of General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can I make one last point, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In this adversarial system, when the Defence specifically and deliberately goes into an area where the witness says, "The Main Staff has no knowledge of anything about this operation," something I stayed away from, they cannot complain that I go into this with documents and material to refresh his recollection. This is the nature -- you must ask questions at your peril. It's the nature of the business. He's opened the door. We are going in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think that the witness said that. On chief, as well as on cross, the witness said that the knowledge and information that they had was based on the reports, which doesn't mean that he didn't know anything about the operations. This is the first thing I would like to point out and the most important thing I'm pointing out. Second of all, you are not familiar with the witness's statement but the Prosecutor was familiar with this statement because on the 11th of July, this was mentioned during the interview and I believe that this is another field that the Prosecutor will go into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is true that to an extent this question flows from previous questions or a line of questions that you've been adopting or pursuing, Mr. McCloskey, but our position, or the position that we take is that we think that we have heard enough on this and we would like you to move to your next point or issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Would it -- can I ask him if he's heard of the operation? I know the map is out. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move. If you want to ask that question, do ask it. I think you can already anticipate what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you're probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, operation Susica, have you heard of that? Pardon my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no mispronunciation. I never heard about it but you see that it has never been either approved or carried out because Krivaja, there would be no Krivaja if this one had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you know about Krivaja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that -- in May, in July 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll get that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness answered yesterday that he did know about Krivaja and he even indicated when he found out about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to comments. There is no reason to comment. And the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She was suggesting that your question was redundant or repetitive. Let's move to the next -- let's finish with this witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware, in the -- on or about the 4th of June 1995, of a Drina Corps attack on the UN operation -- the UN observation post at the edge of the Srebrenica enclave at Zeleni Jadar, where the UN post was taken down and UN soldiers were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can I ask you to see document 2886. And this will be the last document, Mr. President, Witness, everyone. I think. And this is a -- and I'll give you the -- this original, but let me -- it's an April -- excuse me, a 4 June 1995 Drina Corps report to the Main Staff and it's paragraph 3 that I'm interested in. If you could just take a moment to read the document. And it's on e-court, I believe, and --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A detailed report was submitted, in brackets, name by name, brackets closed, about the liberated members of the UN who had been captured in our area of responsibility, through the area of responsibility of the corps there was no passage of the convoy or teams of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So first of all, do you have any recollection of UN soldiers being taken prisoner in the Drina Corps zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To be quite frank, I really don't remember that incident. I don't remember that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, with your leave, of course, I have some and I promise to be relatively quick. First of all I would like to show the witness, in fact we can keep this document for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you just said that you don't remember that incident wherein members of the United Nations force were captured and arrested. Do you remember there was a bombing, there were NATO air strikes, in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know when exactly, May, June. I know that there were air strikes, but I cannot pinpoint them in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember that during the air strikes, certain members of the UN force were taken prisoner, not only in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember something about the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps but I can't remember about the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This recollection that you have that would be in this period, May, June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: All right. Can we show the witness P204? I should like very simply a brief explanation. Would you please look which units are referred to here as addressees? Is it true that this was not addressed to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says exactly the commands of certain units and no Main Staff is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. I was cut off in going to that area. The evidence that I was going to was connecting this document to the Main Staff, and now she is reopening that issue that I was cut off from going to. The map was the connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. Do you wish to comment on that, Ms. Fauveau? Or you are withdrawing the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, I have no other questions on this document. I only wanted to clear up that this witness could not have been aware of this document. I have nothing else to ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position is as it was before, we've heard enough on this. We don't want to hear any more. We have the document, and we proceed from there. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the Witness P45?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you thought this document had been written by General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the last page to the witness? That's the page before this one, with the signature, here. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that this document does not bear the initials of the person who drafted this?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not, and I didn't say definitively that it was Miletic. It's just that there was nobody else in the operations organ, so he was the only one who could have drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you personally, or maybe Colonel Djurdjevic, you sometimes worked in operations, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't work. We helped out. And I don't believe it was Djurdjevic. He had been in the entourage of comrade Tito for 13 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said yesterday that it was not only the practice, it was the rule, that the operations organ followed that the initials of the person who participated in the drafting of the document be put on the document. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. Of course, it was the rule and I wonder why there are no initials here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it possible that this document was written elsewhere, in another sector of the Main Staff, not the operations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's asking for speculation, I believe. This, is it possible? I would agree anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the name General Miletic does not appear as a signatory of this document because General Miletic did not have the powers or authority to sign such a document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. I think this subject is getting very repetitive and he's given his answer several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Our decision is to move to your next question. I think this has been more than sufficiently covered already.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness P5. It's a directive. We need page 15 in B/C/S and 10/11 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, would you bear with me for a while longer? It's going to be my last question. Could you please look at the paragraph concerning the Drina Corps? I'd like to know, is it true that this paragraph refers to different operations, such as Zvijezda, Spreca, Jadar and Prozor, but it does not mention Krivaja operation at all?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. None of these operations were actually effected.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, Ms. Fauveau has suggested -- it's perhaps best that the witness take his ear phones off just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has taken the headphones off. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau has suggested in her questions that UN prisoners could have been taken during the air strikes as they were in other parts of the Drina Corps. I have a very specific document that goes directly to this case that will help answer the question of which UN people we are talking about and it's not UN hostages from the air strikes. Now, I understand this witness may not -- it may not refresh his recollection. That's why I didn't ask him in the first place. But now that on the record there is a suggestion that these UN hostages may have been taken from the air strikes, I have a document that will help this Court figure it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't suggest anything. I asked the question and the witness said that he didn't know any more about the UN force members who were arrested in the area of the Drina Corps after the air strikes apart from this particular incident. I don't see why this is a problem to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one last thing, Mr. President, the only reason I do is that we may come around to this area again but it may be weeks, it may be months, and while we are here and there is a document that is a historic document, and it's as a result of her question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has already indicated his complete ignorance as to the event alleged or mentioned by Ms. Fauveau. So the position is we don't see how you can prove the opposite by introducing this document in the record because if he doesn't know, he doesn't know. So that's not to exclude the importance that this document may have later on, if during the testimony of someone else the incident is referred to, in which case then of course you will come up with that document and it will be more relevant to what that particular witness would be testifying. This one doesn't know anything in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I know all good things must come to an end but I can offer the document from the bar table for whatever the -- Your Honours think it may be worth, though I imagine from your last answer that you don't -- you would like documents to go through witnesses, but as you know, it is a practice that sometimes is done and I think it would help the Court in getting -- as I say, we get to these issues and then we go away from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's difficult to say whatever because I don't know which document we are talking about but in any case, I don't understand why so many problems arise in introducing it through another witness because we are going to hear from other UN witnesses, and they might be able to confirm what the Prosecutor is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's on the list that she got today, just for your information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We stand by our decision. We don't need it now. Later on maybe but not at the moment. Colonel, we have come to the end of a long journey, that being your testimony. We have no further questions for you, which means you can relax now and go back home. Our staff will assist you. On behalf of the Tribunal, but particularly on behalf of my colleagues, Judge Kwon, Judge Prost and Judge Stole, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence in this case. And we all wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I pre-empt the next item which is documents? I would invite the Chamber to postpone submissions on these documents until at least tomorrow. We would like to have a good look at the list and consider our position in relation to those documents that have been used in the course of this re-examination. If the Court would rather it was a day later this week, then that would also be fine, but we will be ready to address the issue tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey? Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As we put things off sometimes we forget about them and everyone remembers this. I just -- the position of the Prosecution is that documents that I presented to this witness, whether or not he knew them or didn't know them, I would like to be in evidence, because I will very likely be arguing that his credibility regarding his knowledge of this operation should be questioned by the Tribunal and that in order for you to understand his answer of "I don't remember this," it's important for you to see what he's not remembering. And these documents will come into evidence, or some of them already are, in other ways, so I'm not trying to bring in a bunch of documents through this witness. This is a practice the Defence have been doing. They have been putting tonnes of documents and asking people about them that they don't flow. If you remember, the Zepa Muslim documents. There were numerous documents. Now, the map, I don't think we ever got to the map so the map is obviously not included in that, in that acceptance, even though I think he answered something on that point but I don't think the map would fit into my argument, but that is my basic view point and I think it fits the practice of the -- of what we have done before and perhaps a little bit of time to look into that practice might be of some help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine. And I mean it. I'm very helpful. All I'm asking is to address the issue at 2.15 tomorrow so I can consider what my learned friend has just said and decide on whether we have any submissions. 2.15 tomorrow afternoon would be absolutely fine so far as the Gvero Defence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as far as the other Defence teams are concerned? All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that we can grant that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will discuss the documents stage tomorrow. In the meantime, Mr. McCloskey, could you be very specific with the Defence teams, indicating which documents you intend to tender with a complete list of the documents you intend to tender with this witness? I tried to mark the ones that used on redirect as you went along but then there were others that you used -- there were others that you used during the direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We'll do that. I didn't get into the July documents because he said that's when the stream of documents started so I didn't -- that's why those weren't used. We will figure that out and get them to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So then documents is postponed until tomorrow at 2.15. We will get the next witness and I need to get --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I just have -- sorry, I just have a preliminary issue with respect to the witness that's -- the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Briefly I just wanted to ask for a caution with respect to this witness and also the witness did raise some unparticularised concerns about his safety which I don't think amounted to sufficient cause to make the request for protective measures, but I wanted to bring that to your attention. There are no protective measures with respect to this witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, I would kindly ask you to make a solemn declaration required by our rules that in the course of your testimony you'll be speaking the truth. Please proceed. Read it out aloud and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will now, if you look at your monitor, if the camera focuses on you, you will see how you are going to appear to the outside world, a bunch of cubes, of colourful cubes. I think we can now start. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. And good evening to you, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good evening to you, sir. I thought I would just start by first asking to you try and keep your voice up during the course of your testimony and also to allow a short pause between the question that I put to you and the answer that you give so that the interpreters have an opportunity to keep up and translate what you say and what I say so that everyone can follow and understand. If I put to you a question that you don't understand, please let me know that and I will do my best to rephrase it in a way that you can understand it and answer it. We only have about 15 minutes left and I know you've been waiting all day so we'll get right to it. If you would, for the record, please, tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: My name Milomir Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, sir, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I was born in Sokolac, Republika Srpska, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what is your present age?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what your educational background is?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I completed the ground forces military academy in Belgrade and the General Staff school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you presently employed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I am currently employed in a private company.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you received any prior military training other than the training that you received in school?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: After my regular schooling, I completed several professional courses in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you a professional military officer throughout your career?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you at some point mobilised into the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that mobilised is a good term. That would be my feeling about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Did you perform duties for the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. From the beginning to the end of the war, I was the commander of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment in the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when did you begin your engagement -- if you can remember, when did you begin your engagement with that particular regiment?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: In early June 1992, I believe. I believe it was either on the 5th or on the 6th of June or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at that time, where was the Protection Regiment headquartered or stationed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: The regiment command was at the command post in the Crna Rijeka sector, the same place where the command post of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, if you could kindly finish at five to 7.00, please, instead of 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your duties and responsibilities were at that time, at the beginning of your engagement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: You're referring to my service in the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, the beginning of your engagement with the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Well, when I was assigned to the unit -- let me just correct one thing. I was first appointed as the Chief of Staff of the Protection Regiment, but since there was no commander, I was simultaneously performing the tasks of the regiment commander and this lasted until the second half of September of 1992. That's when an order was issued appointing me as commander of the regiment. Throughout the war, my main duty was to use the rules, regulations, and to follow the orders of my superior command and all that in the performance of the command over the Protection Regiment. Those were my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the beginning of your engagement, what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at the time of your promotion to commander of the 65th Protection Regiment in September 1992, did you maintain the same rank or did it change?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I was first promoted to the rank of major, and only then was I appointed the regiment commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you maintain that rank throughout your engagement with the 65th Protection Regiment or did it -- or did you receive further promotions along the way?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I was promoted two more times between 1992 and 1995. Those were extraordinary promotions. In 1995, I was promoted to the rank of a colonel. I would like to say that all these three promotions followed incidents in which I was wounded and some combat operations that I had taken part in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us, in brief terms, what the function of the 65th Protection Regiment was in 1995? What was its purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: A Protection Regiment was an atypical unit of the army of Republika Srpska by establishment. Its main task was to provide security for the command post of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, to perform certain other tasks which provided for the normal work of the command of the Main Staff at their main command post in the rear, also to provide security for high officers, and to perform other tasks pursuant to the orders issued by the superior command. I repeat, our main task was to provide security of the command post of the Main Staff and to put in place the conditions for the normal and safe work of the organs of the command of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was one of the functions of the Protection Regiment also to perform military police duties?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Military police duties? Well, the military police performs some of these tasks, i.e. it is predominantly their task to provide physical security of the command post and military officers, also fighting sabotage enemy units. Those would be the main tasks of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I think this is as good a point as any to stop, if that's all right with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we will continue with your testimony tomorrow afternoon. It's important that between now and then, until you finish your testimony, you do not discuss with anyone or allow anyone to approach you to discuss the subject matter of your testimony. Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Have a good evening, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of September, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.54 p.m.,
